justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline anchored around the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, with gentle upward drift built in at each successive horizon. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 133.3 is essentially a near-term mean-reversion assumption — prices tend to cluster around recent levels absent a major catalyst, so the forecast stays close to the last observed price with only a small directional bias. Moving to one week and one month, I applied a slight positive drift consistent with the long-run tendency of equity or commodity assets to appreciate gradually over time, pushing the point estimates incrementally higher to 133.57 and 134.24 respectively. The drift is deliberately small because I had no strong directional signal suggesting a sharp move in either direction.

The confidence interval widths expand considerably as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the fundamental reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, a roughly ±4-point band captures typical intraday and overnight volatility. By one week, that band widens to about ±9 points on each side, incorporating the possibility of several adverse or favorable sessions accumulating. At one month, the ±20-point band reflects not just multi-session price volatility but also the potential for macro regime shifts, earnings surprises, or central bank communications to meaningfully reprice the asset. The width ratios are broadly consistent with a square-root-of-time scaling of volatility, though I applied some additional widening to account for fat tails and the possibility of non-linear market moves.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the upside, a surprise dovish pivot from major central banks, stronger-than-expected economic data, or a sudden resolution of geopolitical tensions could generate rapid appreciation well beyond the upper bound, particularly at the monthly horizon. On the downside, a credit event, an unexpected inflation shock reigniting rate hike expectations, or a liquidity crunch in financial markets could push prices sharply below the lower bound. These tail risks are precisely why the 90% confidence intervals, while wide, still leave 10% of the probability distribution unaccounted for — the most extreme outcomes live in that residual tail and cannot be confidently bounded without more specific information about the underlying asset and current market conditions.
